analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal license to own a handgun or certain semiautomatic rifles and records every sale.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a federal crime to own a handgun or a semiautomatic rifle that takes a detachable magazine unless the owner holds a federal firearm owner license or a certified state equivalent. Getting a license would mean submitting fingerprints and a photo, passing a nationwide criminal background check, paying a fee capped at $10, and renewing every five years. Every sale or transfer of a covered gun would have to run through a licensed gun dealer and be reported to a new federal record-of-sale system, and failing to report a lost or stolen gun or leaving one accessible to a child would become federal crimes punishable by up to 10 years in prison.
analysis.who_benefits: People in communities affected by gun violence, whom the bill's findings say bear disproportionate losses, along with police, who would get a uniform license system and a sale record to trace guns used in crime [S2]. Current gun owners would have two years to obtain a license before the requirement applied to guns they already own [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Every person would need a license, based on rolled fingerprints and a federal background check, before legally possessing a handgun or a semiautomatic rifle with a detachable magazine, with limited exemptions for law enforcement, supervised hunting, ranges, and family settings [S2].

Every sale or transfer of a covered gun would have to be processed by a licensed dealer who verifies the buyer's license and reports the transaction, including make, model, and serial number, to the Attorney General within 14 days [S2].

The bill would create new federal crimes for failing to report a lost or stolen covered gun within 72 hours, failing to notify the Attorney General of an address change within 60 days, and leaving a loaded gun where a child can access it and someone is killed or seriously hurt, with penalties of up to 10 years for licensing violations and 5 years for child-access violations [S2].
The bill would let people denied or stripped of a license appeal, first to the Attorney General and then to a federal judge, who would have to hold a hearing within 72 hours [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Gun owners would pay a license fee (capped at $10), submit fingerprints and mental-health certifications, renew every five years, and face up to 10 years in prison for unlicensed possession of a covered gun. The gun industry would bear new reporting and inspection duties, and private sales would no longer be possible without going through a licensed dealer. The Justice Department would fund and run the licensing and record-keeping system [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun owners and the gun industry

drawbacks.text: Simply possessing a covered gun without a license would carry up to 10 years in prison, so the bill's weight would fall heavily on individual owners rather than only on traffickers or violent offenders [S2].

The bill would repeal the current statutory ban on the Attorney General establishing a firearms registration system and would require dealers to file the make, model, and serial number of every transferred gun into a federal record-of-sale system, which critics of gun regulation describe as a backdoor national registry, even though the bill includes a clause disclaiming a registry [S2].

License applications would require certifications about mental health facility stays and intellectual or developmental disability status, and a license could be denied or revoked on those grounds, raising concerns about stigmatizing people with mental illness; however, an appeal process with counsel and a court hearing within 72 hours is included [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a broad new federal permission system for gun ownership with a traceable sale record, which its sponsor's findings argue addresses the majority of U.S. homicides and roughly half of suicides being firearm-related [S2]. The costs are real and fall on every covered gun owner: a license to exercise what many consider an existing right, criminal exposure for paperwork failures, and a serialized federal sale record. Whether the tracing and screening benefits justify that reach is exactly the fight the bill never got to have.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Duckworth introduced it on May 9, 2024, it was read twice and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Sen. Tammy Duckworth on May 9, 2024 and read twice before being referred to the Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S4].
No further action of any kind appears in the bill's record after the referral to Judiciary [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the bill receiving a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun owners and the firearms industry are better off under the outcome: no federal license or record-of-sale requirement was created, and existing law remains unchanged. The committee that never took it up avoided a politically difficult vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun owners and the gun industry

for.name: Tammy Duckworth
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and named it for Blair Holt, a Chicago student killed on a school bus in 2007; it was her only Senate action on the bill before it stalled.

against.name: Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee to which the bill was referred, never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill's record shows no committee action after the May 9, 2024 referral [S4].

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no senator of either party signed on as a cosponsor, so the only measurable support was the Democratic sponsor's own introduction [S3].

industries.note: Every private sale or transfer of a covered gun would have to run through a licensed dealer, who verifies the buyer's license and files the transaction, creating a mandated new stream of transfer business [S2]. Dealers would also bear new record-keeping, reporting, and inspection duties and would face customers who resent the added cost and delay.

A licensing requirement could shrink the pool of people who can legally buy handguns and semiautomatic rifles, while the bill adds production and sales reporting duties and lets the Attorney General inspect manufacturing premises [S2]. Manufacturers' interest in unrestricted sales runs against the bill's public-safety aim, though a dealer-must-process rule would not change their retail channel much.
